title: Für Elise
about: Beethoven wrote this short piano piece in 1810, and his manuscript names it for Elise. Nobody knows for sure who Elise was. Ludwig Nohl found the piece and published it in 1867, forty years after Beethoven died.
funFact: One theory says Nohl misread the name, and the piece was really written for Therese Malfatti, whom Beethoven hoped to marry.

practice.text: Play the first four bars with the right hand alone, and let the song wait for each note.
Play the right hand alone from bar 5, where the hand moves down to middle C.
Now the left hand alone. It holds two shapes, one per bar.
Put both hands together on the first eight bars.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: Rock between fingers 5 and 4 for E and D sharp, like a gentle swing.
The left hand waits here. Play the tune softly, as if telling a secret.
Lift the hand in the rest after A, and land with the thumb on middle C.

tricky.text: Your thumb takes the black key G sharp, so the hand can reach up to C.
After the rest, your thumb lands on middle C. Look down before you play it.
The hand moves down to middle C again. Use the rest in bar 12 to get there.

practice.text: Play the right hand alone, slowly, on the first eight bars.
Play the left hand alone. Each chord climbs from the bass, one note per beat.
Join the hands on bars 4 to 8, where they take turns.
Play the whole song with both hands, a little slower than written.
Now play it at full speed.

tips.text: The left hand climbs, then the right hand carries on climbing. It should sound like one hand.
Thumb on E, little finger on the high E. Spread the hand over the whole octave.
G sharp in the bass makes the chord bright. It pulls the ear back home to A.

tricky.text: The left hand opens wide: finger 2 plays B, and the thumb reaches up to G sharp.
The same stretch as bar 6: finger 2 plays B, and the left thumb reaches up to G sharp.
Use the rest after A to move the right thumb down to middle C.

practice.text: Play the Alberti bass alone until it rolls by itself: low, high, middle, high.
Play the right hand's thirds alone, and press both notes of each pair as one.
Join the hands on bars 4 to 8, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed, with the pedal.

tips.text: Keep the Alberti bass soft, so the tune sings above it.
Change the pedal on every bar line. Lift it as the new bass note sounds.
The tune is the top note of each third, so let the upper finger lead.

tricky.text: Lift the hand after the thirds, then land with the thumb on middle C and the little finger on A.
The same jump as bar 20: thumb on middle C and little finger on A, together.
Spread the hand for the last chord: thumb on C, finger 2 on E and finger 4 on A.

practice.text: Play the stride bass alone: jump down for the octave, then back up for the chord.
Play the right hand's chords alone, and let the top finger sing the tune.
Join the hands on the second half, where the tune climbs an octave.
Play the whole song with both hands at three-quarter speed.
Now play it at full speed, and let the last chord ring.

tips.text: In stride, look at the bass note and let the hand find the chord by feel.
Up high, the E and D sharp should shimmer. Keep them light and even.
Play the top note of each chord a little louder than the others.

tricky.text: The four-note chord comes back. Lift off the high C first, then land on the whole octave.
Lift the hand off the high C, then grab A, C, E and A with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 5.
The left hand's chord on beat two has only E and G sharp. Add B on beat three.
